Article Title: Microsoft is hiring a legal engineer to teach lawyers across the company how to…
Article Text:
Microsoft wants a lawyer who can build AI agents, and it is paying up to $278,900 for one

Why Microsoft wants a lawyer who can also write software

The legal engineer job is spreading from startups to Big Tech

Microsoft has spent the past two years telling everyone else that AI is about to change how work gets done. Now it wants someone to prove the point inside its own legal department. The company has posted a job for a principal legal engineer, an unusual hybrid role that asks for a practising attorney who can also ship software, with base pay topping out at $278,900 a year.The listing, spotted on LinkedIn this week by Business Insider, puts the hire inside Microsoft's Customer & Partner Solutions group, the arm that supports the company's commercial business. The work is deliberately hands-on: building AI agents, sharpening prompts, and training attorneys and paralegals to actually use the tools. "This is a role for a builder," Microsoft wrote in the job description, adding that the person will partner directly with engineering rather than advise from the sidelines. Microsoft did not respond to Business Insider's request for comment.Lawyers were the corporate world's great tech holdouts for decades, understandably nervous about tools that could get one detail wrong in a 90-page agreement. That resistance is thinning. Clients are now pushing outside firms toward tools like Harvey and Claude for Legal to turn work around faster and bill less for it.The same pressure has moved in-house. Legal teams are betting that software can handle contract edits and policy drafting, letting them keep more of the early work and hand outside counsel matters that are already halfway done.Microsoft has a head start here because it builds some of these tools itself. Its lawyers already use Copilot for routine work, including contract review, where it compares a draft against similar agreements, flags issues and suggests edits that match company policy. Harvey is being rolled out across Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs.Until recently, legal engineer was mostly a startup title, filled by ex-lawyers with technical chops who sat close to customers. Palantir posted its own embedded legal engineer role last month, promising to turn manual workflows into automated ones.Microsoft wants a law degree and at least seven years of practice. Experience with Harvey or Copilot is preferred. Base pay starts at $147,000.
Article Summary: Microsoft has posted a job for a principal legal engineer, an unusual hybrid role. It asks for a practising attorney who can also ship software, with base pay topping out at $278,900. The work is deliberately hands-on: building AI agents, sharpening prompts, and training attorneys.

Article Title: Apple Beats 360 headphones leak with new design, six colours and $299 price
Article Text:
Beats 360 to get a new design

Beats 360 may be offered in six colours

Beats 360 price and features

Apple’s unreleased Beats 360 over-ear headphones have allegedly appeared on several retail websites, revealing details about their design, colours, features and pricing ahead of an official launch. Listings for the headphones were spotted on Amazon U.K. and other retail websites before being removed. The leak suggests that the Beats 360 will have a new design compared with the current Beats Studio Pro and Solo 4. The headphones are expected to offer active noise cancellation, all-day battery life, IPX4 water and sweat resistance and support for both Apple and Android devices. Retail listings have also revealed a $299 US price.The leaked images show the Beats 360 with a different design from the company's existing over-ear headphones. The headphones feature a separate padded section underneath the headband, while the earcups have a more open mesh design.The padded section can reportedly be removed, as can the ear cushions. Retail listings also mention an Extra Cushion Kit, with Performance Knit and UltraPlush options. The leaked headphones also appear to be the same model that football player Lamine Yamal was seen wearing in Instagram posts earlier this summer.The Beats 360 is expected to launch in Sky, Black, Navy, Cloud, Pink and Volt. The six colour options would give the headphones a wider range of finishes than the current Beats Studio Pro and Solo 4.The Volt version has a bright neon-yellow finish.Retail listings have also revealed pricing. One listing showed the headphones at $299, while another listed them at £331.99. The Beats 360 is expected to feature active noise cancellation, with one product description claiming up to 1.75 times more noise cancellation than the Beats Studio Pro.The headphones reportedly do not use Apple's H2 chip or another Apple chip. They will, however, work with both Apple and Android devices. The headphones were also listed with an IPX4 rating for water and sweat resistance.The leaked product information claims the Beats 360 can offer all-day battery life even with ANC turned on. The headphones are said to fold flat and are expected to come with a woven ripstop fabric carrying case.
Article Summary: Listings for the headphones were spotted on Amazon U.K. and other retail websites. The leak suggests that the Beats 360 will have a new design compared with the current Beats Studio Pro and Solo 4. The headphones are expected to offer active noise cancellation, all-day battery life, IPX4 water and sweat resistance and support for both Apple and Android devices.

Article Title: ChatGPT can now send texts for Mac users with new Apple Messages plug-in, but why they need to be careful about using this feature
Article Text:
What the new ChatGPT feature actually does

Why this could be a sensitive move for Apple

How OpenAI says it's handling privacy

What users actually have to enable

OpenAI has rolled out a new Apple Messages plug-in for its popular chatbot ChatGPT on Mac, enabling the AI system to read, write and send texts directly through iMessage. The integration also allows ChatGPT to search conversations and generate summaries, expanding its functionality beyond productivity apps like Notes and Xcode. OpenAI stressed that the feature requires explicit user consent and runs locally on the Mac, using AppleScript and Accessibility tools to interact with the Messages app. During setup, users encounter multiple opt‑in menus, including a permissions screen confirming that on‑device message history will be accessed.The new ChatGPT plug-in introduced by OpenAI will enable the chatbot to conduct direct actions within the Apple Messages app. ChatGPT will be able to read, wrote and also send text messages on the behalf of the user. Along with this, it will also be able to search through the existing messages and create summaries or also pull other information out of conversations, effectively giving ChatGPT hands-on access to a core piece of Apple's messaging ecosystem.According to a report by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has built much of its brand identity around strong privacy protections, and the company has historically been especially protective of the contents of users' messages.A tool built by a third-party AI company, one capable of processing Apple customers' message data through OpenAI's own systems, is the kind of feature likely to draw scrutiny from privacy advocates and, potentially, from Apple itself. An Apple representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the launch.The timing adds another layer of tension: the feature arrives amid an already strained relationship between the two companies. Apple sued OpenAI last month, accusing the AI firm of stealing information related to upcoming Apple products.In response to questions about the new integration, OpenAI emphasised that the feature requires explicit user consent and does not build an index of a person's entire message history. The company said the plug-in runs locally on the Mac itself, relying on existing macOS tools such as AppleScript and Accessibility features to interact with the Messages app, rather than routing message data through a separate indexing system.Setting up the integration isn't a single toggle. When a user first configures it, ChatGPT displays a permissions screen explaining that the app will access the computer's on-device message history. Beyond that in-app consent step, users also need to adjust several privacy settings directly within the Mac's System Settings app, including enabling a feature called Full Disk Access. Users must additionally grant ChatGPT permission to access contact names and automation tools, a setup process similar to what's required to enable other AI-based automation software, such as Codex Computer Use.This isn't OpenAI's first foray into pulling personal data from Apple's ecosystem. The company recently added support for analyzing data from a user's iPhone or iPad Health app as well, though Apple's iOS and iPadOS include a built-in permission step specifically requiring users to approve sharing that health data with ChatGPT before it can proceed.
Article Summary: OpenAI has rolled out a new Apple Messages plug-in for its chatbot ChatGPT on Mac. The feature will enable the AI system to read, write and send texts directly through iMessage. The integration also allows the chatbot to search conversations and generate summaries. OpenAI stressed that the feature requires explicit user consent.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Fraudster uses Raigad SP’s WhatsApp display photo to dupe police staff, seeks Rs 50,000
Article Text:
A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers, but the scam attempt was foiled. (AI-generated image)





NAVI MUMBAI: Raigad Cyber Police have registered a case against an unidentified fraudster who allegedly used the WhatsApp Display Picture (DP) of Raigad Superintendent of Police (SP) Anchal Dalal to deceive several police personnel into transferring money.On Thursday, the fraudster sent a message to Raigad SP's reader, PSI Siddheshwar Murkute, asking him to transfer money urgently. Murkute immediately realised that it was a modus operandi commonly used by cyber scammers, as the WhatsApp message was sent from an international number that was not saved in his mobile phone.Thereafter, PSI Murkute learnt that the same scammer had sent similar messages to several Raigad police personnel. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters.Subsequently, PSI Murkute registered an FIR against the unidentified accused under the relevant section of the BNS for the offence of cheating by personation.The complainant, PSI Murkute, said, "I had received the WhatsApp message from an international number and the DP was of Raigad SP Anchal Dalal.The message read, 'I am in a meeting and my mobile is switched off. Immediately transfer Rs 50,000 to my bank account.' I knew the message sender was a scammer. I deliberately replied asking for the bank account number by pretending to send the money. As I received the bank account number from the scammer, it will be useful for the cyber police team to trace the bank account holder. "PSI Murkute added, "One police officer had received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam and claiming that it was required for filling diesel in the car, and that her mobile battery had drained and she was unable to pay online at the fuel station."API Amol Jadhav of Raigad Cyber Police said, "The cyber scammers use VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) to mask their identity. However, the Internet Protocol (IP) address of the WhatsApp number used by the accused will be obtained to trace the location, and the accused will soon be behind bars."
Article Summary: A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters. One police officer received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam.

Article Title: Part-time online job scam: Senior citizen duped of Rs 24.93 lakh in Tamil Nadu
Article Text: COIMBATORE: A 62-year-old man in Coimbatore district was cheated of Rs 24.93 lakh in a part-time online job scam.According to police, V Subburaj, 62, of Pollachi received an advertisement on the Telegram messaging app offering a part-time job involving hotel booking and writing reviews on hotels. A cyber fraudster, using the Telegram handle @Miaaaana577, enticed Subburaj to create user IDs on malicious sites (including hotings.vip and httngt.com) and complete assigned tasks.The fraudster promised lucrative profit margins and instructed Subburaj to make a deposit to assign him tasks. He also promised that once the task was complete, the deposit amount along with the profit would be transferred. Believing this, he transferred a total sum of Rs 24,93,940 in 41 online transactions into various suspect bank accounts provided by the fraudsters.When he attempted to withdraw his earned profit, the scammers demanded an additional “tax payment.” Realising he had been duped, the man lodged a complaint with the district cybercrime police on Wednesday.Based on the complaint, police registered a case under sections 318(4) and 319(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Section 66(D) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, and started an investigation.
Article Summary: A 62-year-old man in Coimbatore district was cheated of Rs 24.93 lakh in a part- time online job scam. V Subburaj, 62, of Pollachi received an advertisement on the Telegram messaging app offering a job. A cyber fraudster, using the Telegram handle @Miaaaana577, enticed him to create user IDs on malicious sites.

Article Title: Japan installed a 1.1 MW turbine beneath the Naru Strait, using predictable tidal currents to generate clean electricity for the Goto Islands
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How Japan’s 1.1 MW AR1100 tidal turbine generates electricity underwater

Image AI generated

Japan’s tidal energy project grows from a 500 kW pilot to a 1.1 MW turbine

Why predictable tidal energy could complement solar and wind in Japan

The engineering challenges of operating a tidal turbine underwater

Between Japan’s Goto Islands, the sea is doing something that is usually associated with wind farms and solar fields. Beneath the surface of the Naru Strait, a 1.1 MW turbine is drawing energy from water moving with the tides and sending electricity back towards land through a subsea cable. No blades are turning in the sky and no panels spread across the shoreline. The machine works largely out of sight, following currents whose timing can be forecast well in advance. Installed by Proteus Marine Renewables, the AR1100 grew from an earlier 500 kW trial in the same waters. Its deployment has given Japan a megawatt-scale tidal system designed to work with the regular rise and fall of the sea rather than depending on sunshine or changing winds.The project also demonstrates the potential of tidal power in narrow channels, where fast-moving water can provide a concentrated source of renewable energy. By placing the turbine underwater, the system avoids taking up large areas of land while tapping into a resource that follows a predictable natural cycle.The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water and no set of panels covering land.The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection. According to Proteus Marine Renewables, the turbine was deployed in February 2025, while later company information recorded that it received Japanese certification and began exporting electricity to the grid in June 2025.The arrangement is fairly straightforward in principle, although operating it beneath the sea is not. The rotor extracts energy from moving water, the drivetrain passes that mechanical power to a permanent-magnet generator, and the resulting electricity is carried to an onshore station. A yaw system turns the nacelle as the tidal flow reverses, while independently controlled blades can alter their pitch to regulate how the turbine responds to changing conditions. AR1100 is a horizontal-axis turbine mounted on a gravity-based support structure. The earlier project in the same strait provided the starting point for the larger machine.Offshore Energy reported that the earlier 500 kW AR500 pilot operated in the Naru Strait with 97% availability in 2021. That earlier machine had a rated capacity of 500 kW and recorded 97% availability during its operation, according to the material released about the project. The experience allowed engineers to see how the technology behaved in the actual marine environment rather than only in controlled testing.The next version increased the rated capacity to 1.1 MW and introduced changes to the turbine's control systems. An equipment supply and works contract with Kyuden Mirai Energy was signed in November 2022, with the Japanese project subsequently moving towards the upgraded machine. Advanced pitch and yaw systems were incorporated as part of the work. The company says those changes were intended to improve the turbine's performance and efficiency while allowing it to deal more effectively with the changing direction of the tidal flow.The most distinctive feature of tidal power is not simply that the turbines sit underwater. It is the predictability of the resource. Solar output changes with daylight and weather conditions. Wind can strengthen, weaken or stop altogether. ClickPetroleogas noted that tidal production can be estimated in advance because the cycles follow predictable natural patterns, unlike renewable generation that is more affected by weather conditions. The electricity produced at any particular moment still depends on the conditions at the site and the performance of the equipment; the underlying movement of the water is far less of a surprise.That distinction matters when renewable sources are being combined. A grid operator cannot make the sun shine or order the wind to blow, whereas the timing of tidal cycles can be incorporated into generation planning. It does not make tidal energy constant; the flow rises and falls as the tide changes, but it makes the pattern easier to anticipate. For islands such as those around the Goto group, where space and fuel logistics can present particular constraints, a submerged source can sit alongside solar, wind and other forms of generation. The Naru Strait project is intended to contribute to reducing emissions from the islands' electricity supply.Underwater generation creates its own engineering problems. Components have to survive saltwater, strong currents and long periods of exposure while remaining accessible enough for inspection and maintenance. Getting people and equipment to a submerged turbine can also require vessels, specialist crews and careful planning. The location itself has to provide sufficient water movement, suitable depth and a practical route for sending the electricity into the grid.The Naru Strait project therefore depends on more than the turbine turning. Its subsea cable links the machine to an onshore electrical station, where the generated power can be processed for distribution. Local vessels and resources were used during deployment, with Proteus' offshore team overseeing the work, while Kyuden Mirai Energy and Japan's Ministry of Environment have been involved in advancing the project.There is also a useful way to think about the long-term promise of the machine, without treating its output as something that can be guaranteed hour by hour. The tidal timetable itself is highly predictable. Engineers can calculate when stronger and weaker currents are expected well into the future, creating a generation pattern that can be plotted ahead of time. What cannot simply be printed on that chart is the turbine's actual electricity production for every future hour: maintenance, operating conditions and other technical factors still matter.That distinction is important. The Naru Strait turbine is not a giant power station, nor does the available source material establish that it will produce a fixed amount of electricity every hour for a decade. What the project demonstrates is something more specific: a megawatt-scale machine can be installed beneath a Japanese strait, connected to shore and operated using an energy source whose basic timing is known far in advance. The water will keep changing direction. The turbine is built to follow it.
Article Summary: The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water and no set of panels covering land. The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection.

Article Title: In 2017, Germany’s Freiburg opened a city hall with solar-powered walls designed to produce more energy than the building needs
Article Text:
Image: World Green Building Council

Freiburg’s newest town hall was designed as an energy-producing building

Freiburg’s newest town hall was designed as an energy-producing building (Image: AI Generated)

Solar panels cover the parts of the building exposed to sunlight

Its insulation and ventilation systems help keep energy demand low

The building produces more electricity than it needs

Freiburg turned everyday government architecture into a renewable-energy showcase

A city hall where the building can give electricity back

In Freiburg, south-west Germany, a city hall has been designed to do something unusual for a government building: produce more energy than it consumes. Completed in 2017, the city’s latest town hall combines high-performance solar panels with an energy-efficient design that sharply reduces the building’s demand for heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting. The World Green Building Council lists City Hall Freiburg at Fehrenbachallee and describes it as a surplus-energy building, noting that photovoltaic units on the roof and sun-exposed parts of the façade generate more electricity than the building requires. The project goes beyond simply adding solar panels to an existing office. Its insulation, ventilation, heating and cooling systems were designed together as part of a wider energy concept. Freiburg’s official tourism site also notes that construction began in 2014 and that, after completion in 2017, the building was expected to generate more energy than it needed.The building is located at Fehrenbachallee in Freiburg, Baden-Württemberg, rather than at the historic Rathausplatz associated with Freiburg’s older town halls. The World Green Building Council identifies its construction/refurbishment date as 2017 and records its address as Fehrenbachallee, Freiburg, Baden-Württemberg 79106, Germany.That distinction is useful because Freiburg has several buildings referred to as town halls. The city’s official tourism website explains that the latest town hall was constructed between 2014 and 2017, while the older New Town Hall is a much earlier Renaissance complex. The modern building was therefore created specifically for contemporary administration, with energy performance incorporated into its architecture from the beginning. Rather than treating electricity generation as an addition, its designers made renewable energy and low consumption central to the building's operation.One of the most distinctive elements of the project is the way photovoltaic technology has been incorporated into both the roof and façade. The roof and areas of the façade exposed to direct sunlight are fitted with high-performance solar energy panels. These panels have a dual function: they generate electricity while also shielding parts of the building from direct solar radiation. That approach makes the building itself part of its energy infrastructure. Instead of requiring a separate solar farm or relying entirely on rooftop space, the architecture provides additional surfaces for electricity generation. The strategy is particularly relevant in urban areas, where land can be expensive and limited. Freiburg’s latest town hall demonstrates how walls and roofs that would normally serve only structural or protective purposes can also contribute to a building’s energy supply. The result is a structure where renewable-energy production is visible in the architecture rather than hidden away.Producing large quantities of solar electricity is only half of the building’s energy strategy. Freiburg’s town hall was also designed to need less energy in the first place. The building has outstanding thermal insulation that permits low-temperature heating and high-temperature cooling. Its ventilation system incorporates heat recovery, reducing the amount of energy lost through the movement of indoor and outdoor air. The building also uses groundwater as part of its heating and cooling strategy. A heat pump operates the heating system, while a plate heat exchanger provides cooling. These systems work alongside the building envelope and ventilation system rather than functioning as isolated technologies. This integrated approach is important because an energy-positive building cannot depend solely on generating more electricity. Its performance also depends on controlling how much energy is required to maintain comfortable conditions for the people working inside.The combination of low energy demand and substantial photovoltaic generation gives Freiburg’s town hall its defining characteristic. The World Green Building Council describes it as Europe’s biggest surplus-energy building and says its photovoltaic units produce more electricity than the building needs. The surplus does not simply disappear. The building can respond to requirements from the electricity network and feed excess electricity back into the grid. This means the town hall can function not only as an energy consumer but also as a small-scale producer contributing electricity beyond its own immediate needs. The concept changes the traditional relationship between buildings and power systems. Instead of a building continuously drawing electricity from an external network, the building can generate renewable power, satisfy its own requirements and return excess generation to the wider system.The project is particularly striking because it applies advanced energy principles to an ordinary civic function. A city hall is primarily a workplace for public administration, yet Freiburg’s building has been designed to demonstrate what that workplace can achieve environmentally. The project is recorded under its net-zero operational carbon category and holds a DGNB Climate Positive certification. Freiburg's official tourism information places the project within the city's broader collection of town halls, but the 2017 building represents a sharp contrast with the historic structures. The older buildings reflect centuries of civic and architectural history; the latest one reflects a contemporary attempt to reduce the environmental cost of running a large public building. Its significance therefore lies not simply in the number of solar panels installed, but in how architecture, insulation, ventilation, heating, cooling and renewable generation were brought together into one energy concept.Freiburg’s modern town hall demonstrates a different way of thinking about public buildings. Instead of designing a structure that simply consumes energy and then adding solar panels afterwards, the project combines low demand, renewable generation and energy-efficient systems from the outset. The building generates more energy than it requires for heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting, with surplus electricity capable of being fed into the grid. That makes the building more than an administrative workplace. Its roof and sun-facing façade generate power, its insulation reduces energy loss, its ventilation system recovers heat, and its heating and cooling systems make use of groundwater. Together, these features turn Freiburg’s town hall into a practical demonstration of how public architecture can contribute to the energy transition. Rather than merely occupying space within a city, the building actively produces some of the energy that the city and its occupants depend upon.
Article Summary: Freiburg’s newest town hall was designed as an energy-producing building. Solar panels on the roof and sun-exposed parts of the façade generate more electricity than the building requires. insulation, ventilation, heating and cooling systems were designed together as part of a wider energy concept.

Article Title: China’s 16.18-km undersea high-speed rail tunnel completes 21-day cutter replacement under extreme pressure
Article Text:
Image: AI Generated

How China’s Jintang undersea tunnel completed high-pressure shield cutter replacement

Engineers replaced 104 cutting tools under high pressure

The “Deep-Sea Space Station” allows longer work shifts

China is pushing high-speed rail through underwater environments

Deep beneath the waters off eastern China, engineers are carrying out one of the most demanding stages of construction on a high-speed railway tunnel. The Jintang undersea tunnel, part of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway in Zhejiang Province, has completed the inspection and replacement of 104 shield cutting tools after 21 days of work under intense water and soil pressure. The 16.18-kilometre tunnel is set to become the world’s longest undersea high-speed rail tunnel, linking Ningbo with Zhoushan and cutting the journey between the two cities from as much as two hours to about 26 minutes. The latest operation also tested a domestically developed saturation hyperbaric system adapted from deep-sea diving technology. The achievement comes as China continues pushing high-speed rail construction through challenging underwater environments, including the recently completed shield-machine crossing beneath the Yangtze River, another major engineering milestone highlighted by China’s State Council Information Office . The operation demonstrates how construction methods are being adapted to underwater conditions safely too.The Jintang tunnel is the critical undersea section of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway and stretches 16.18 kilometres, including an 11.21-kilometre shield-bored section. It will connect the port city of Ningbo with the Zhoushan islands, where journeys currently rely heavily on roads and ferries. Once the railway opens, travel between Ningbo and Zhoushan is expected to take as little as 26 minutes, compared with roughly 1.5 to 2 hours today.The tunnel is being excavated from opposite shores using two super-large-diameter shield machines. One machine, Yongzhou, must bore 4,940 metres through 24 alternating layers of soft and hard rock, representing nearly 70 per cent of its route and creating severe wear on its cutting tools. Excavation progress is being monitored carefully. The geological conditions make the project particularly demanding. Rock strength along the route reaches 191 megapascals, placing some of the material in the high-strength to very-high-strength category. As the cutting head moves through alternating rock layers, its tools experience substantial mechanical stress and wear. That made the latest replacement operation necessary, but carrying out such maintenance deep beneath the seabed presented a challenge of its own. At the tunnel’s deepest point, the excavation reaches about 92 metres below sea level, where combined water and soil pressure can reach 8.5 bar. A roughly 2,000-metre section experiences pressure above 6 bar. These conditions mean that workers cannot simply enter the cutting chamber using conventional methods and carry out maintenance as they would in a normal tunnel.The latest operation involved inspecting and replacing 104 shield cutting tools over 21 days. These tools sit at the front of the tunnel-boring machine and are responsible for breaking through the rock and soil ahead of it. Their condition is critical because worn cutters can reduce excavation efficiency and make continued tunnelling more difficult. The operation was carried out under high water pressure, turning what would ordinarily be a demanding mechanical maintenance job into a complex human-safety challenge. Global Times reported that conventional compressed-air methods provide workers with only around 40 minutes of effective working time per person each day and are generally limited to depths of approximately 60 metres. The Jintang tunnel’s deeper and higher-pressure conditions required a different approach. The construction team spent three years adapting technology derived from deep-sea saturation diving. The result was described as China’s first domestically developed saturation hyperbaric system for shield tunnelling, nicknamed the “Deep-Sea Space Station” by the project team. Rather than repeatedly exposing workers to major pressure changes, the system allows them to remain in a controlled pressurised environment for extended periods.The system consists of living, transfer and control modules designed to allow workers to operate safely under the extreme conditions surrounding the tunnel boring machine. The system can accommodate nine workers for extended periods, with crew members travelling to the work face through a transfer chamber. They can work for up to eight hours at a time, allowing round-the-clock multi-shift operations for as long as 28 days. One of the key advantages is that workers undergo a single controlled decompression after completing their assignment instead of repeatedly moving between normal atmospheric pressure and the high-pressure working environment. This reduces the risks associated with frequent pressure changes and makes prolonged underwater construction work more manageable. The technology represents an unusual overlap between offshore engineering and underground construction. Techniques developed for people working at significant depths underwater have been adapted to create a controlled environment inside a tunnel-boring operation. In practical terms, the system gives engineers more time at the cutting face while reducing the number of dangerous pressure transitions workers must endure. The successful 21-day cutter replacement operation therefore represents more than routine maintenance. It provided a real-world test of whether the new system could support prolonged work under the pressure conditions encountered by the Jintang tunnel.The Jintang project forms part of a broader expansion of high-speed rail infrastructure through some of China’s most challenging terrain. The Ningbo-Zhoushan railway is designed to bring Zhoushan more directly into the national high-speed rail network, with the undersea tunnel providing a crucial connection beneath the water separating the islands from mainland Zhejiang. The project also comes shortly after another major underwater railway milestone in China. On July 31, 2026, the State Council Information Office reported that China had completed excavation of the tunnel beneath the Yangtze River for the Shanghai-Chongqing-Chengdu high-speed railway. The project uses the large-diameter shield machine Linghang and is designed for high-speed trains travelling at up to 350 kilometres per hour without slowing for the underwater section.The two projects involve different waterways and engineering challenges, but together they demonstrate the scale of China’s efforts to extend high-speed rail through difficult underwater environments. While the Yangtze project required a record-setting shield machine to pass beneath one of the country’s largest rivers, the Jintang project is tackling prolonged excavation beneath the seabed, where high rock strength and intense pressure complicate both boring and maintenance. For the Jintang tunnel, is also another step towards completing a connection expected to dramatically shorten travel between Ningbo and Zhoushan. The Yongzhou shield machine has already advanced 3,936 metres, or nearly 80 per cent of its assigned task. If construction continues as planned, the finished tunnel will not simply provide a faster route between two cities. It will also stand as a demonstration of how large-scale rail infrastructure can be built in environments where conventional tunnelling techniques reach their limits, with workers and machines operating beneath some of the most challenging pressure conditions encountered in modern rail construction.
Article Summary: Engineers replaced 104 cutting tools under high pressure. The Jintang undersea tunnel is part of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway in Zhejiang Province. The 16.18-kilometre tunnel is set to become the world’s longest undersea high- speed rail tunnel.

Article Title: Archaeologists find earliest physical evidence of brass-making in East Asia in southern China
Article Text:
Archaeologists find the earliest physical evidence of brass-making in East Asia in southern China (PC: Cambridge University Press)

Ancient crucibles reveal early brass-making in medieval China

Ancient crucibles reveal early brass-making in medieval China (PC: AI Generated)

How did ancient craftspeople make brass from copper and zinc

How did brass-making technology reach medieval Guangzhou

What does the discovery reveal about medieval metallurgy in China

A set of ancient crucibles found in Guangzhou is giving archaeologists new clues about how brass-making technology may have reached medieval China. The vessels came from an official metallurgical workshop at the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom and dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD. Their metal residues show that craftspeople were producing brass locally through cementation rather than simply working with imported objects. According to a research article published by Cambridge University Press, titled ‘ Brass technology transmission via maritime routes: crucible evidence from southern China ’, points towards wider technological connections with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was a major trading port, and the authors suggest maritime routes may have helped move metallurgical knowledge across regions. The study analysed crucibles using chemical, microscopic and lead-isotope methods. Together, the findings provide direct archaeological evidence for medieval brass production in southern China and offer clues about how the technology may have travelled.Archaeologists found three well-preserved brass-making crucibles at an official metallurgical workshop in Guangzhou. The workshop was part of the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom site and was active across many centuries.The three crucibles belong to the ninth–tenth century group. Each was cup-shaped with a slightly inward-sloping rim and a rounded base. Some had a pouring spout. They measured about 60-80 mm across and 60-70 mm high, with a capacity of roughly 0.2-0.3 litres. Researchers found heavy heat damage and glassy material on their surfaces. Metal residues inside included copper, zinc compounds and brass droplets. A nearby semi-subterranean furnace also dates to the seventh-tenth centuries. Together, these remains provide direct evidence of metalworking at the site.The crucial evidence came from residues left inside the crucibles. Microscopic and chemical analyses identified zinc oxide, zinc silicate, and droplets of brass. One group of crucibles contained high-purity copper and binary brass droplets with about 11-17% zinc. Another contained bronze with tin alongside zinc and produced a copper-zinc-tin alloy. The researchers interpret these residues as evidence for cementation. In this process, zinc-bearing material is heated with copper or a copper alloy so zinc enters the metal and forms brass. The remains therefore show more than the presence of finished brass objects. They preserve traces of the production process itself.The study also examined lead isotopes to investigate the likely origin of the raw materials. The three analysed crucibles had similar lead-isotope ratios that fit signatures associated with the Cathaysia tectonic province. Because these signatures occur widely across southern China, the researchers say a local source for the raw materials is reasonable. The technology itself may have travelled from farther west. The authors point to similarities between the Guangzhou crucibles and brass-making vessels associated with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was also a major international trading port. Historical evidence records connections between the city and Arab merchants. The researchers therefore suggest that maritime routes and the movement of merchants and craftsmen may have helped transmit brass-making knowledge to southern China.The findings add important evidence to the history of brass production in China. Local brass production is generally thought to have begun around the tenth century AD, but the Guangzhou crucibles provide direct evidence from the ninth-tenth centuries. The researchers argue that the discovery helps explain how a specialised metallurgical technique became established locally. It also shows why archaeological workshops can reveal details that written records alone cannot provide. The study does not claim that every element of brass technology came from one place or through one route. Instead, it highlights a possible connection between western technological traditions, maritime trade and local production in Guangzhou. The evidence adds an important piece to the history of metallurgy in East Asia.
Article Summary: Archaeologists found three well-preserved brass-making crucibles at an official metallurgical workshop in Guangzhou. The crucibles dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD. Their metal residues show that craftspeople were producing brass locally through cementation rather than simply working with imported objects.

Article Title: Singapore rebuilt a vanished 1920s lake inside a new housing estate; engineers turned it into a flood-control system and wildlife habitat
Article Text:
Singapore revived the memory of a 1929 landmark

The lake is actually a giant stormwater reservoir

A lake that changes its job when it rains

Wetlands help turn the infrastructure into a living landscape

The housing estate was designed around nature too

Singapore has brought the memory of a vanished 1920s landmark into one of its newest housing estates, but the new Alkaff Lake is doing much more than recreating a piece of the past. Built inside Bidadari Park, the 1.8-hectare lake was inspired by the former Alkaff Gardens, which opened to the public in 1929. Today, it doubles as a stormwater retention pond designed to reduce flood risk while also serving as a recreational and natural space for residents. During heavy rain, the lake can hold up to 40,000 cubic metres of water, roughly the equivalent of 16 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Its wetlands, swales and surrounding greenery also help cleanse stormwater and provide a habitat and stopover area for wildlife.The story of Alkaff Lake goes back to 1929, when the Alkaff family, a prominent Arab merchant and landowning family in Singapore, opened Alkaff Gardens to the public in the Bidadari area. The gardens became a popular attraction and were known for their landscaped surroundings and recreational spaces. Decades later, as Bidadari was redeveloped into a new residential estate, planners decided to incorporate elements of its history into the new neighbourhood. The modern Alkaff Lake does not restore the original garden or recreate an identical historic lake. Instead, Singapore's agencies say it was designed to pay homage to the former Alkaff Gardens and recreate their sense of tranquillity while giving the site a new practical function.The most unusual feature of Alkaff Lake is what happens during a downpour. The lake sits at the lowest point of Bidadari and is designed to receive runoff from about 43.5 hectares, or roughly half of the estate. It can temporarily store as much as 40,000 cubic metres of water, equivalent to about 16 Olympic-sized swimming pools. When heavy rain arrives, water is diverted into the lake rather than flowing immediately into downstream drains. Outlet points then control the rate at which the stored water is released, slowing the flow and reducing pressure on the downstream drainage system. PUB developed the arrangement partly because the downstream drain could not simply be widened further due to space constraints.On an ordinary dry day, Alkaff Lake looks like a conventional urban waterbody, with landscaped banks, viewing areas and recreational space for the surrounding community. During intense rainfall, however, its role changes into that of a temporary stormwater storage facility. PUB says the lake's normal water level is typically maintained between 1 and 1.5 metres, but it can rise to around 4 metres during heavy rain as it captures excess runoff. Water-level sensors are connected to warning beacons and audio announcements in four languages, alerting visitors to move away from the lake when the water rises. The design therefore allows the same piece of land to function as public space during normal conditions and flood-control infrastructure during storms.The lake was designed using Singapore's Active, Beautiful, Clean Waters, or ABC Waters, approach, which seeks to integrate water management with attractive public spaces and natural features. Alkaff Lake contains terraced wetlands, swales and a cascading creek that help slow and cleanse stormwater before it enters the lake. Gross Pollutant Traps capture litter and sediment carried by runoff, while aerators improve water circulation and increase dissolved oxygen in the lake. The surrounding park also contains greenery, trails, viewing decks and a nest-shaped shelter overlooking the water. Rather than hiding the drainage infrastructure underground or behind concrete barriers, the design makes the water-management system part of the landscape that residents can actually see and use.Alkaff Lake forms part of the much larger Bidadari Park, which occupies more than 10% of the Bidadari estate and was developed around the idea of a "Community in a Garden". The park was planned to preserve the area's natural character while providing recreational space for the surrounding housing developments. Planners retained an approximately 1-hectare hillock as a stopover site for migratory birds and created a land bridge connecting it with the main park area. The bridge also creates a route for people and wildlife between the green spaces. Authorities have recorded species including the collared kingfisher, yellow-vented bulbul and pink-necked green pigeon using the bridge, while butterfly-attracting plants and other vegetation have been incorporated into the landscape.
Article Summary: Alkaff Lake was inspired by the former Alkaff Gardens, which opened to the public in 1929. During heavy rain, the lake can hold up to 40,000 cubic metres of water, roughly the equivalent of 16 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Its wetlands, swales and surrounding greenery also help cleanse stormwater and provide a habitat and stopover area for wildlife.

Article Title: "Was the footage edited?": Candace Owens demands answers from Blake Neff over bizarre SD card footage after Charlie Kirk shooting
Article Text:
Candace Owens (Image via Getty Images)

Candace Owens asks Blake Neff about SD cards, edited footage and what happened after Charlie Kirk was shot

Candace Owens clashes with Blake Neff over Tyler Robinson defense filings

Candace Owens has reignited debate surrounding the Charlie Kirk murder investigation after publicly questioning footage that she says raises questions about what happened at the crime scene. In a post directed at TPUSA spokesman Blake Neff, Owens focused on SD cards allegedly handled shortly after Kirk was shot and asked whether the footage had been edited. Her comments add another layer to an already heated public dispute over the case.Owens directly tagged Blake Neff and demanded an explanation for footage that she believes deserves closer scrutiny. The screenshot shows her asking why Tarryl allegedly did not turn SD cards over to the SBI and why he appeared to place one in his pocket before putting it into a computer shortly after Charlie Kirk was shot.Owens wrote:“Hey @BlakeSNeff— can you please respond to let people know why Tarryl didn’t hand the SD cards he took from the crime scene over to the SBI or why he appears to put the SD card in his pocket followed by popping it into his computer — within about 10 minutes of Charlie getting hit.Was the footage edited?Seems like a very odd thing to do in the immediate aftermath.Also while I have you, you certainly made the public believe that after calling your mom you guys hightailed it to the hospital after. But that’s not exactly true, is it, Blake?Do you remember what you did?”The wording is significant because Owens is not simply discussing the broader case.She is pointing to a specific sequence shown in footage and asking whether its presentation accurately reflects what happened.Her questions remain allegations and questions raised by Owens, rather than established findings. The screenshot itself does not establish that footage was edited or that anyone mishandled evidence. Those points would require confirmation from investigators or other reliable evidence.Still, the post highlights how individual pieces of video continue to fuel competing interpretations of the Charlie Kirk case. It also shows that Owens is directly challenging people she believes have presented an incomplete version of events.The dispute comes as Owens and Neff have also clashed over the legal proceedings involving Tyler Robinson, who is accused in Kirk’s killing.Neff recently argued that Robinson’s defense filings did not challenge key evidence described by prosecutors. He pointed to camera footage, DNA, the rifle, the cause of death and phone data while questioning why the defense had not raised theories promoted by Owens.Neff wrote:“Utah prosecutors have responded to Tyler Robinson's defense filing ahead of the final preliminary hearing, and confirms what observers pointed out about that filing: The defense is very conspicuously not contesting any of the core evidence showing Tyler Robinson committed the murder. They don't contest the camera footage, the DNA, the rifle, the cause of death, or Tyler's phone data.”He added:“All they have is a complaint about reliable hearsay (which won't apply at the full trial anyway) and then attacks on the aggravating factors. If there was any merit at all to any of the theories that Candace et al. have pushed the last 11 months, why didn't the defense bring them up?”Owens pushed back sharply, arguing that Neff misrepresented what a preliminary hearing is designed to determine. She said:“Blakey. He's already been community noted on it for its intentional misrepresentation. He just lies and misrepresents and we're the bad guys for noticing that he's doing it.”She also argued:“I guess community noted before I can even reply because it's it's it's stunning to me that he thinks he can get away with this. It says preliminary hearings decide only probable cause under the Utah 112 standard. Um uh reliable hearsay is allowed. Defense council often skip alternative theories to avoid previewing their strategy before the trial,”The latest SD card questions now give the Owens-Neff dispute another focal point, with the authenticity, context and interpretation of footage likely to remain central to the online debate.
Article Summary: Candace Owens asks Blake Neff about SD cards, edited footage and what happened after Charlie Kirk was shot. Her comments add another layer to an already heated public dispute over the case. Owens and Neff have also clashed over the legal proceedings involving Tyler Robinson, who is accused in Kirk’s killing.

Article Title: In 1972, a Florida man started building a retirement home in a swamp; decades later, it became a 12,000-square-foot castle
Article Text:
Image: Inhabitat

How Howard Solomon turned a Florida swamp into a 12,000-square-foot castle of folk art

How Howard Solomon turned a Florida swamp into a 12,000-square-foot castle of folk art (Image: FOX 13 Tampa Bay)

Why Solomon’s Castle is covered in discarded newspaper printing plates

From retirement home to Florida’s strangest roadside castle

In 1972, Howard Solomon set out to build a quiet retirement home in rural Florida, but the land he chose was far from ordinary. Instead of a conventional building site, he found a swamp, yet the challenging terrain did little to discourage him. Solomon adapted his plans and began constructing upwards, slowly transforming the property into a striking three-storey, medieval-style castle. What started as a personal home-building project continued for more than four decades, expanding into a remarkable 12,000-square-foot maze of towers, stained glass, sculptures, workshops and curious handmade details. The castle’s most distinctive feature is its gleaming exterior, which gives the structure an almost otherworldly appearance. Rather than using conventional siding, Solomon covered much of the building with discarded aluminium printing plates that had once been used by a local newspaper. The unusual material was inexpensive, durable and perfectly suited to his passion for transforming unwanted objects into imaginative works of art.Solomon bought his land in 1972 after returning to the United States from the Bahamas, choosing an inexpensive stretch of Florida wilderness near Ona.As per Atlas Obscura, he had initially envisioned a more conventional home, but the swampy ground made building horizontally difficult. Rather than abandon the project, he changed direction and began constructing upwards. The result gradually took on the appearance of a medieval fortress, complete with turrets, a drawbridge, towers and a moat. The building was never designed from a finished architectural plan. Solomon worked on it incrementally, using his skills in woodworking, metalwork, glass and construction to transform his ideas into physical form. What began as a retirement home became a constantly evolving piece of folk art. By the time of his death in 2016, the structure covered around 12,000 square feet and had become both a home and a gallery for his creations.The castle's extraordinary silver exterior is what makes it immediately recognisable. Instead of conventional stone or brick cladding, Solomon covered the structure with aluminium offset printing plates discarded by a local newspaper. The unusual material gave the building a bright, metallic appearance, while allowing Solomon to transform something destined for the rubbish into part of his enormous artwork. The idea was particularly suited to Solomon's approach to making art from objects other people no longer wanted. He used reclaimed materials throughout the property, turning junk and industrial leftovers into sculptures and architectural details. The printing plates were reportedly purchased for just 25 cents apiece, making them an inexpensive solution as well as a creative one. Over time, thousands of these plates became part of the castle's identity, their blank surfaces reflecting Florida's intense sunlight.Solomon's project eventually became much more than a private residence. The castle developed into an attraction filled with his whimsical sculptures, many assembled from discarded machinery, automotive parts, oil drums, wood and other found objects. His creative philosophy was simple, keep making things and find another use for materials that others had thrown away. The property also grew beyond the main building. A 60-foot replica of a 16th-century Portuguese galleon sits in the moat and became the Boat in the Moat restaurant, while the grounds contain additional artworks and unusual structures. The castle's interior became a gallery of Solomon's work, preserving decades of experimentation under one roof. What makes Solomon's Castle remarkable is that it was never simply intended to imitate a medieval fortress. It was a personal experiment that kept expanding for decades. A retirement home built on difficult swampy ground became a shining three-storey landmark, proving that an impractical idea can sometimes become an extraordinary work of art.
Article Summary: Howard Solomon set out to build a retirement home in rural Florida in 1972. Instead of a conventional building site, he found a swamp, yet the challenging terrain did little to discourage him. Solomon adapted his plans and began constructing upwards, slowly transforming the property into a striking three- storey, medieval-style castle. The castle's most distinctive feature is its gleaming exterior, which gives the structure an almost otherworldly appearance.

Article Title: Man claims Meta fired him after he refused to sign a Green Card letter for a Chinese visa worker, seeks $1 million in lawsuit
Article Text:
A man has filed a lawsuit against Meta claiming that he was fired after he declined to sign a Green Card letter for a Chinese visa holder as his manager. He said he found the claims made in the letter questionable.

What is EB-2 NIW Green Card?

James Tillinghast, a former Meta employee, has filed a lawsuit against the company, claiming that he was fired after he refused to sign a letter seeking Green Card for a Chinese employee in 2024. The lawsuit said that the letter that Tillinghast refused to sign contained factual assertions that he believed were materially inaccurate. The letter was intended to support an I-140 National Interest Waiver petition for Shenxum Wang. The names were disclosed in the lawsuit, as reported by HRDive, Breitbart etx.Wang apparently worked within Tillihast's unit and his signature was required for the application. Going by the lawsuit, around April-May 2024, Meta and an immigration law firm coordinated an I-140 EB-2 National Interest Waiver petition (Green Card) for Wang. A proposal was prepared for managerial reference and it attributed $683 million in incremental advertising revenue to Wang.Tillinghast did not have data to confirm that Wang personally generated that amount. The letter also implied that Wang had created algorithms or AI tools.James was unsure about that too and James understood that Wang's actual role was in product design and user experience.The lawsuit claimed that the letter stated that Wang managed, led, or oversaw a team or cross-functional group, which Tillinghast did not agree. Tillinghast worked with Wang to revise the letter so that it contained only statements that the manager could truthfully endorse and he declined to endorse the broader statements about national importance of Wang.A few months after his refusal to sign the letter, Meta fired the manager. The termination documents for the manager “did not identify underperformance as the reason for termination,” per the complaint. “Meta later advanced an oral underperformance explanation that Plaintiff contends was pretextual.”Tillinghast in his lawsuit has asked for a little over $1 million in damages, including $565,000 in lost pay and $490,000 in lost equity. He has also asked for punitive damages and a jury trial in New Jersey.Meta has not issued any statement regarding the lawsuit.The EB-2 National Interest Waiver is a Green Card pathway that allows certain professionals to apply without being sponsored by a US employer. Instead of relying on a specific job offer, the applicant must show that their future work in the United States serves the national interest. NIW emphasizes what you plan to do and why it matters to the country as a whole. It is suitable for researchers, engineers, entrepreneurs, and professionals whose work is not confined to a single employer or role.
Article Summary: James Tillinghast, a former Meta employee, has filed a lawsuit against the company, claiming that he was fired after he refused to sign a letter seeking Green Card for a Chinese employee in 2024. The letter was intended to support an I-140 National Interest Waiver petition for Shenxum Wang. A few months after his refusal to sign the letter, Meta fired the manager.

Article Title: Meet Vallabh Ramesh, the 18-year-old Kentucky student who created a 3D-printable smart gel that solidifies at body temperature and could one day deliver drugs inside the body
Article Text:
Vallabh Ramesh's work looks at how next generation materials could be used in drug delivery, tissue engineering and other areas of biomedical technology in the future.

A smart gel with a trigger of temperature

From 3D printed jaws to drug delivery

Beyond the medicine

The young researcher also explored potential uses for the gel outside biomedical applications. (Image: Society for Science)

A young mind with larger mission

Designing the future

Science and technology has never failed to surprise humans. Think, what if you could print a material into virtually any shape, respond to temperature, and one day help deliver medicine inside the human body? Sounds impossible? Well, it is possible! For 18-year-old Vallabh Ramesh, that question became the catalyst for an ambitious science project. According to Society for Science, Ramesh, a duPont Manual High School student, developed a smart polymer gel that can be 3D-printed with relatively inexpensive equipment and that undergoes a change at body temperature. His work looks at how next generation materials could be used in drug delivery, tissue engineering and other areas of biomedical technology in the future. Scroll down to read the details.Smart materials are designed to respond to changes in their environment. Depending on their composition, they can respond to stimuli like temperature, light, pressure or electrical signals. Ramesh’s materials science project was on a thermo-responsive polymer gel – a material that changes properties with temperature. By repeatedly experimenting he identified concentrations of different components that would allow the gel to be processed with more accessible 3D-printing technology.This is important since many advanced smart materials require specialized and expensive printers to make complex structures. His goal was to see if a less expensive way could make these materials easier to handle, states the report.Ramesh started by printing structures such as jaws to demonstrate the potential of his material. The prototypes demonstrated that the gel can be formed in complex shapes and not just used as a flat or uniform material. Then he turned to a more biomedical application. Ramesh used the gel to make little “pouches,” which would be designed to release chemicals slowly over time. The experiment was a proof of concept for the potential construction of a similar material for controlled drug delivery. The concept could have implications for personalized medicine, as treatments are increasingly being developed around individual patients and their specific needs. But a lot more testing and development would be needed before the medical application could become a reality, clarfies the online report.The young researcher also explored potential uses for the gel outside biomedical applications. His experiments proved the material could be used as a heat sink, and could potentially help deal with heat generated by electronics. He also tested its electrical conductivity and found his gel to beat some commercially available gels in his testing. These experiments hint at the wider promise of smart polymers. Materials that respond to their environment can potentially be adapted for fields ranging from medicine to electronics and robotics, rather than being limited to one application.Ramesh is not just interested in laboratory experimentation. He leads the school’s rocketry team at duPont Manual High School, merging engineering and science with real-world design and problem solving. He has been working on a project on social and community connectedness. Ramesh founded a school club which grew into Cognitive Connections, a nonprofit that sends volunteers to visit seniors in care facilities and supports fundraising efforts for dementia research. His work reflects an interest in using technology and community initiatives to address real world problems.Ramesh also has a creative passion outside of science and engineering: digital design He loves making wallpapers and experimenting with visual styles inspired by early 2010s tech esthetics. That combination of scientific curiosity and design might be appropriate for someone who works with 3D-printable materials. Ultimately his project is to imagine what materials could do differently, and find a practical way of making those ideas tangible. At 18 years old, Ramesh is already probing questions at the intersection of materials science, medicine, electronics and engineering. His smart gel is still a research project, not a medical product, but the possibilities show how young researchers are using accessible technologies to explore problems that used to be the preserve of sophisticated laboratories.Images Courtesy: Society for Science
Article Summary: Vallabh Ramesh, 18, developed a smart polymer gel that can be 3D-printed with relatively inexpensive equipment and that undergoes a change at body temperature.
