Article Title: Meet Lianna Genovese, an 19-year-old Canadian student whose gadget made from straws, sponge and pipes helps people with cerebral palsy rediscover painting; now sells in over 25 countries
Article Text:
The will to change lives

“I wanted to give Elissa back her passion,” recalled Genovese.

3D printer-inspired system that guides hand movements

Different objects can be attached at the end, such as a pen, marker, brush, or a stylus for touch screens.

Beyond an experiment

In 2023, Genovese was also included in the Forbes 30 Under 30 Local Toronto list.

An estimated 18 million people of all ages live with cerebral palsy across the globe. Within the United States, this number ranges from 764,000 to 1 million, with about 1 in every 345 children diagnosed, according to the Cerebral Palsy Guide. Most such kids are unable to entertain themselves with the toys and activities that others their age do. But one Canadian student's invention has helped children with cerebral palsy venture into the art of painting.Straws, pipe cleaners, and sponges would seem of no use to an engineering student other than their one true purpose. But for Lianna Genovese, they sparked an idea that went beyond her room into hospitals, schools and homes in dozens of countries. The inspiration came when she met Elissa, introduced through the James Dyson Award and McMaster University as a woman with cerebral palsy who had lost the ability to use a brush and subsequently, her ability to paint as she once did. Genovese was only 18, a first-year student and studying biomedical and mechanical engineering at McMaster University in Canada. They met through a classroom project where Genovese and her classmates were working to help Elissa.While other students focused on an ergonomic computer mouse or other daily-use items, Genovese’s group members looked for a way to help the avid artist paint again. “I wanted to give Elissa back her passion,” recalled Genovese. Upon learning of Elissa's story, she began thinking of ways to leverage the movements that the woman was still able to perform to guide a brush across a surface. In a statement made by the university in 2021, Genovese explained that hearing about the story ignited her desire to restore part of Elissa's capacity for expression.This is when she formed a principle that formed the base of the final project: using larger movements of the arm and shoulder to compensate for the limitations of fine hand movements. According to the James Dyson Award and McMaster University, the first prototypes were assembled with straws, pipe cleaners, and a sponge. She collaborated with Elissa who participated in testing and provided feedback on what she could or could not do with the equipment.Based on these experiences, new versions began to emerge. The project continued to be refined with the involvement of individuals with differing medical conditions, along with neurologists and occupational therapists. By 2021, Lianna had already spoken to or tested with more than 150 patients and healthcare professionals in Canada, according to McMaster University.Two years later, the university reported that the development had already received contributions from more than 525 occupational therapists, neurologists, and individuals with limited hand mobility.The most advanced version of Guided Hands adopted a logic reminiscent of the movement of a 3D printer. The device has a structure made up of linear axes and bearings that allows for guided hand movement. With this, the user can perform horizontal and vertical movements and also change the direction of the motion. The person rests their hand on an adapted piece and moves the whole setup mainly using the larger motor skills of the shoulder and arm. Different objects can be attached at the end, such as a pen, marker, brush, or a stylus for touch screens.It does not paint or write on its own and rather functions as a structure that supports and guides the movement performed by the individual themselves. This ensures that the user's participation is vital.Among the tests conducted during the development, one meeting changed Genovese's thoughts on the device. She met Bella, a girl with cerebral palsy and observed her using Guided Hands to write, colour, draw and play on an iPad. According to the engineer, watching the girl’s reaction made her realise that this college project could have much broader applications beyond the classroom.The experience helped transform an academic activity into a venture. She founded ImaginAble Solutions in 2019, while she was still a third-year student, to develop and commercialise assistive technologies. In an initial phase, the very structure used to develop the product operated in the basement of the young entrepreneur’s home, according to a report published by McMaster.In August 2021, Genovese won the Canadian stage of the James Dyson Award, an international design and engineering competition aimed at students and recent graduates. She secured the national prize of US$3,500 to further develop the invention and also qualified the device for the international phase of the competition.At that time, the expectation was to bring the equipment to market by the end of 2021. However, commercial development continued through testing and programs with hospitals and rehabilitation centres. McMaster later reported that the product officially entered the market when Lianna graduated in 2022.What started as inexpensive materials assembled to test a movement is now being manufactured in the Hamilton region of Ontario and distributed internationally.Moreover, in 2023, Genovese was also included in the Forbes 30 Under 30 Local Toronto list. In 2024, she received the Muhammad Ali Humanitarian Award for her work on inclusion and quality of life for people with disabilities.
Article Summary: Lianna Genovese developed Guided Hands to help children with cerebral palsy. The device uses a structure reminiscent of a 3D printer to guide the user's hand movements. It has been used in hospitals, schools and homes in dozens of countries.

Article Title: Apollo 11 set up the Moon's first seismometer in 1969; its recorded moonquakes gave scientists the first detailed map of the lunar interior
Article Text:
Buzz Aldrin and Apollo 11 Lunar Lander. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Short but memorable period

Constructing the detailed map

Results From the Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment

A timeless basis for continued discoveries

When Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the Sea of Tranquility in July 1969, they deployed several scientific instruments during their moonwalk, including one designed not to study rocks or footprints but to detect seismic activity on the Moon. It was a seismometer, the first instrument placed on another world to detect the equivalent of earthquakes. That single, short-lived experiment marked the beginning of lunar seismology, a field that eventually let scientists build a detailed picture of what lies beneath the Moon's surface, though it took data from several later missions, not Apollo 11 alone, to complete that picture.The instrument Armstrong and Aldrin deployed was called the Passive Seismic Experiment. As described on NASA's official science page for the device , it packed four separate seismometers, three long-period sensors and one short-period vertical sensor, into a single unit powered by two solar panels. The device was also sensitive enough to measure the vibrations produced by the movement of the astronauts as well as the activities of people around the lander. When activated, it sent seismic measurements back to receiving stations on Earth, enabling researchers to examine the magnitude, duration, and origin of the events.Because it was powered by sunlight and lacked thermal control, it could operate only during lunar daytime.This, along with the intense lunar noon heat, ended the experiment. NASA's report states that the instrument package ceased responding to commands at 0400 UT on 25 August 1969, probably due to overheating.Twenty days might seem insignificant, but that period was enough to show that seismology could be applied to other celestial bodies. In its description of the scientific findings from the Apollo program, NASA mentions that the Passive Seismic Experiment discovered moonquakes and provided scientists with information about the internal structure of the Moon, as summarized on NASA's astrobiology mission page . During its short operational life, the same instrument detected an estimated 100 to 200 meteorite impacts, while the later Apollo network detected 1,700 meteoroid impacts over a longer service period.Recognizing the value of the short dataset, NASA developed improved designs for the instrument. The later seismometers were powered by radioisotope thermoelectric generators, fitted with improved thermal regulation, and installed at the Apollo 12, 14, 15, and 16 landing sites. In contrast to the Apollo 11 instrument, the more advanced seismometers deployed at the Apollo 12, 14, 15, and 16 landing sites operated as a long-duration network and transmitted data to Earth until September 1977, according to the NASA Astrobiology mission page for Apollo 11.The map we have today of the Moon’s interior was built from this joint effort, which began with Apollo 11. NASA technical report from the mission's science teams,, available through the NASA Technical Reports Server , documents how researchers used the accumulated seismic data to trace how energy from moonquakes and impacts traveled through the Moon's crust, mantle, and core, revealing a layered interior with a crust, mantle, and core, while also showing that the Moon is smaller, less seismically active, and thermally more evolved than Earth.Over almost eight years, this network recorded many thousands of seismic events, including deep and shallow moonquakes, artificial impulses, and more than a thousand meteoroid impacts. The most common type of moonquake was the deep kind, which occurred hundreds of kilometers below the surface and repeated at specific phases of the Moon’s tidal cycle. Another, rarer type of moonquake was the shallow kind, which occurred closer to the surface and may have been caused by tectonic activity within the lunar crust. Analysis of wave propagation and attenuation helped scientists understand the thickness of the lunar crust, distinguish it from the mantle below, and detect the presence of a tiny core inside the Moon, information that could not have been discovered by Apollo 11 alone in just 20 days.More than fifty years later, the information gained from Apollo 11’s initial measurements and the subsequent missions remains a source of discovery. Modern researchers re-evaluate the old records using up-to-date methods of computation, finding signals that were not analyzed properly before. While Armstrong and Aldrin’s passive seismology experiment during their first spacewalk on the Moon was small-scale and short-lived, it helped launch an entire field of study.
Article Summary: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin deployed a seismometer on the Moon in 1969. It was the first instrument placed on another world to detect the equivalent of earthquakes. The instrument was powered by sunlight and lacked thermal control, so it could operate only during lunar daytime. NASA's report states that the instrument package ceased responding to commands at 0400 UT on 25 August 1969.

Article Title: In 2014, New York completed the Javits Center’s bird-safe renovation and green roof; bird collisions fell by more than 90%, while 65 species later used the roof
Article Text:
The Javits Center’s glass facade alongside a bird, highlighting New York’s effort to make the building safer for migrating birds. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

How a glass building became safer for birds

The Jacob Javits Convention Center in Midtown Manhattan. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

How the green roof became a stopover for birds

The Jacob K. Javits Convention Center in Manhattan was once one of New York's most dangerous buildings for birds. Its large glass facade reflected the sky and surrounding vegetation, making the building difficult for migrating birds to see as an obstacle. During the centre's major renovation, completed in the early 2010s, thousands of glass panels were replaced with low-reflection, fritted glass that makes the surface more visible to birds. At the same time, the project added a 6.75-acre green roof, creating a stretch of vegetation high above Manhattan. Monitoring by the NYC Bird Alliance , formerly known as NYC Audubon, found that bird-building collisions at the centre fell by more than 90% after the glass was changed. The roof then became a stopover where migrating birds could feed and rest.The two changes solved different problems. The glass was meant to keep birds from hitting the building, while the roof gave them somewhere to use in a city dominated by concrete, roads and tall buildings. The green roof was planted mainly with sedum and other low-growing vegetation, creating habitat unlike the hard surfaces around it. When biologists began monitoring the roof in 2014, they were not simply checking whether birds visited.They were building a long-term record of which species used the new habitat and how use changed over time.Before the renovation, the Javits Center was a major collision hotspot. Birds moving through Manhattan during migration could see reflections of trees and sky in the facade and fly toward what appeared to be open space. The renovated building used patterned and less reflective glass instead. The Javits Center's sustainability information says more than 6,000 bird-friendly glass panels were installed and that bird collisions fell by more than 90% after the work.The change did not require removing the building's glass facade altogether. Instead, the new panels incorporated a frit pattern that helped make the surface visible to birds. That approach later became an important example in New York's push for bird-friendly building design. The centre became a case study for how a large glass building could remain useful and visually open while reducing a major danger to migrating birds. The green roof added another part to the story. It turned the top of the convention centre into a patchwork of plants where birds could find insects, shelter and rest. As monitoring continued, the list of recorded species grew.Over the years, the roof became more than an experiment in urban landscaping. Birds began using it as a stopover habitat during migration, while resident species also appeared. Monitoring included visual surveys, acoustic recordings and camera traps, allowing researchers to track wildlife that might otherwise have gone unnoticed. By February 2023, NYC Bird Alliance had recorded 51 bird species on the Javits Center’s network of green roofs. Its current project information lists a cumulative total of 65 bird species, along with five bat species and representatives of 18 arthropod orders. The organisation’s records also include native bees, butterflies and other insects.What it can do is offer a small patch of habitat where wildlife can find food and shelter while moving through one of the country's most built-up areas. The researchers have also found signs of interactions between species living there. Their monitoring has included bats feeding on moths, while birds use the vegetation and insects around it. The roof has become a small urban food web, not just a decorative garden.The project also showed why bird-safe glass and green roofs are effective together. Preventing collisions reduces the danger created by the building itself, while the roof gives birds a place to land after they have crossed the city. Neither change solves the wider problem of habitat loss or the many hazards birds face during migration, but together they changed what had once been a particularly hostile part of Manhattan.More than a decade after the renovation, the Javits Center offers an example of how an existing city building can be redesigned for wildlife without losing its original purpose. The convention centre still hosts huge events below, while above it, birds and other animals use a rooftop that did not exist as habitat before the renovation. What started as an effort to reduce collisions became something larger: a building that is safer for birds and a rooftop habitat that supports wildlife during migration. The Javits Center shows that bird-friendly design can serve two purposes at once. Visible glass patterns reduce the chance of fatal collisions, while vegetation above the building provides food, shelter and resting space. The roof cannot replace larger natural habitats, but it demonstrates how urban infrastructure can be redesigned to make room for wildlife.

Article Title: Around 1830, America imported Japanese wisteria for its hanging purple flowers; the vigorous vines can now smother trees and compete with native vegetation
Article Text:
Japanese wisteria (Wisteria floribunda) covered in hanging clusters of its purple flowers. Credits - WIkimedia Commons

Wisteria floribunda

How a garden vine reached the woods

Wisteria sinensis

A mature Japanese wisteria vine displaying its long, cascading purple flower clusters. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

When ornamental flowers signal invasion

Around 1830, Japanese wisteria arrived in the United States as an ornamental plant, prized for its long, fragrant clusters of purple flowers.was planted around homes, gardens and porches because of its striking spring display. For generations, it remained a popular garden vine. But some plants escaped cultivation and reached nearby forests, where the same vigorous growth that made wisteria attractive in gardens gave it a very different role. The USDA Forest Service identifies Japanese wisteria as a nonnative invasive vine and places its introduction to the United States around 1830.Once it reaches a forest, Japanese wisteria can weave through shrubs and climb into the canopy. Its woody stems wrap around trunks and branches, while its dense leaves shade plants growing below. Older vines can become heavy enough to weigh down trees, and tight coils around trunks can limit their growth. The Invasive Plant Atlas notes that Japanese wisteria can girdle trees and shrubs and alter forest vegetation by reducing the light available to native plants.Many infestations have developed close to old gardens and homes, where ornamental vines escaped into surrounding woodland. Japanese wisteria can spread through seeds, but stems that touch the ground can also produce roots and new shoots. That allows a single established plant to spread outward and form a larger patch without relying on new seedlings. Once a vine has reached nearby trees, it can use them as support and move quickly into the canopy.That growth can make the plant particularly difficult to remove. Cutting back the visible vines may leave roots and older stems alive, allowing fresh shoots to appear later. Pulling out a large vine can also be difficult when its stems have become tangled through shrubs and tree branches. In established infestations, land managers often have to return repeatedly to control regrowth.Japanese wisteria is not the only Asian wisteria growing in American landscapes. Chinese wisteria,, was introduced even earlier, and both species now grow outside cultivation in parts of the southeastern United States. Because the two species can hybridise, some wild plants may show a mixture of their characteristics, making identification and management more difficult. For forests, the key point is the same: once these vigorous vines escape into natural areas, they can spread far beyond the garden where they were planted.The flowers are one of the easiest ways to recognise a wisteria vine, but they do not always identify the species with certainty. Long clusters of purple, pink or white blooms hang from the vine in spring, which is one reason these plants became popular with gardeners. Distinguishing Japanese wisteria from Chinese wisteria or hybrids may require examining additional features, such as the direction in which the vine twines and the structure of its leaves and flower clusters.Dense vine growth can cover branches, block sunlight and make it difficult for native plants beneath the canopy to compete. Young trees may struggle to grow, while mature trees supporting large vines can become weakened or weighed down. The Alabama Cooperative Extension System recommends repeated cutting and other control measures for invasive wisteria, noting that established plants can be persistent once they have spread into wooded areas. Early detection is therefore important. Small plants can often be removed more easily before their stems reach nearby trees and their roots become established. Once a vine has entered the canopy, control becomes more difficult because managers must protect surrounding vegetation while preventing new growth from returning.Nearly two centuries after Japanese wisteria was introduced for its flowers, the plant is now viewed very differently outside cultivated gardens. Its ability to climb, shade and tightly wrap around other vegetation allows it to spread through forests and compete with native plants. What began as an attractive addition to American landscapes became an invasive vine capable of changing the structure of the forests it invades. The flowers may still be beautiful, but in a forest they can signal that the vine has spread beyond the garden and begun overtaking nearby trees.
Article Summary: Japanese wisteria was introduced to the United States in 1830. It is a nonnative vine that can spread into forests. It can cover branches, block sunlight and make it difficult for native plants beneath the canopy to compete. Once a vine has reached nearby trees it can use them as support and move quickly into the canopy.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:

Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: Google rejigs AI leadership as DeepMind CEO shifts role
Article Text:
The shake-up comes during a pivotal juncture for Google DeepMind: the flagship version of its latest Gemini model remains unreleased

Google parent company Alphabet on Wednesday announced a leadership overhaul of its AI division, with AI chief Demis Hassabis leaving his main managerial role and as several leaders of its Gemini model, including veteran engineer Jeff Dean, left the company to launch a startup called Discovery Loop. The shake-up comes during a pivotal juncture for Google DeepMind: the flagship version of its latest Gemini model remains unreleased despite a planned June launch, sparking investor and industry concerns that Google is falling behind its rivals Anthropic and OpenAI, each of which scooped up a star Google AI staffer this summer.Shares of Alphabet fell 4% after the news. Hassabis, a Nobel Prize recipient, will take the newly created title of Alphabet’s chief scientist and transition from being Google DeepMind CEO to being its chairman, he said in a memo to staff.Koray Kavukcuoglu, the unit’s chief technology officer, will assume day-to-day responsibilities of DeepMind in addition to his parallel role as Alphabet’s chief AI architect.
Article Summary: Google parent company Alphabet on Wednesday announced a leadership overhaul of its AI division, with AI chief Demis Hassabis leaving his main managerial role. Hassabis, a Nobel Prize recipient, will take the newly created title of Alphabet’s chief scientist and transition from being Google DeepMind CEO to being its chairman.

Article Title: Apple layoffs hit employees across teams; company confirms job cuts, says: While we will create new roles as part of this change, it will also...
Article Text:
Apple has laid off more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro

Apple Vision Pro layoffs: gaming team shut down, immersive video crew cut back

Siri job cuts explained: new AI architecture needs a different kind of engineer

Apple smart glasses take priority as Vision Pro waits for 2028

Apple has laid off more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro, according to a Bloomberg report by Mark Gurman. The split is roughly even. About 100 roles have gone from the Vision Pro organisation, and about 100 more from Siri and the software groups around it. Also caught in the round is Intelligent Systems Experience, a team inside Apple's software engineering arm that builds AI features sitting across iPhone, iPad and Mac.Apple confirmed the cuts without confirming the number. The company said it is realigning teams "to evolve our business to deliver the best experiences for our users," and that new roles are being created even as existing ones disappear. Staff who lost jobs can apply elsewhere inside Apple. What makes this round worth reading closely is that one headcount figure is hiding two completely different stories. One team is being rebuilt. The other is being told to wait.The headset took the harder blow. Apple has largely closed the group working on Vision Pro gaming and shrunk the team producing immersive video, the 3D content Apple has used as the device's showpiece since launch. That content is expensive in a way the sales figures could not support.A single episode can run into several million dollars, shot by multiple crews of Apple staff and contractors, for an audience that stayed small. AppleInsider reported the first wave a day before Bloomberg, putting at least 60 layoffs across Apple's VR teams. Films like Submerged will still get made, just fewer of them, with outside studios expected to pick up the slack. Gaming never arrived at all. The most capable VR workaround on the platform, iVRY, still needs a Windows PC plugged in to work.Siri's situation is the opposite of a wind-down. The assistant is being rebuilt on a new technical architecture for its AI version, and that stack asks for skills the old one did not. So some roles end, resources move, and new positions open around the rebuilt assistant. Apple showed the revamped Siri at WWDC this year and a public beta is due before 2026 closes. Nobody cuts a team weeks before shipping unless the team they need looks different from the one they have.Vision Pro arrived in February 2024 at $3,499 and now sells for $3,699, close to Rs 3.2 lakh, after component costs forced a rise. Heavy, costly, thin on reasons to wear it daily. Apple insists visionOS is not going anywhere, and visionOS 27 shipped in June to prove it. A new headset is still penciled in for as late as end-2028. Meanwhile Bloomberg reports work with Samsung Display on an entry-level XR display was suspended, and Apple is aiming to announce smart glasses at WWDC 2027 and ship them that year. Those glasses will not run immersive video or heavy games.Incoming CEO John Ternus now owns the decision. Apple has not given up on a screen you wear on your face. It has given up on this one being the version people buy.
Article Summary: Apple has laid off more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro, according to a Bloomberg report. Apple confirmed the cuts without confirming the number. The split is roughly even. About 100 roles have gone from Vision Pro organisation, and about 100 more from Siri and software groups around it.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jack Dorsey: “Everyone has an idea. But it’s really about executing the idea and…” - simple lesson about taking the first step
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jack Dorsey

“Everyone has an idea. But it’s really about executing the idea and attracting other people to help you work on the idea.”

What Jack Dorsey meant by the quote

Why having an idea is only the beginning

The role of other people in turning ideas into reality

Jack Dorsey’s early interest in technology

How Dorsey turned a simple payment idea into Square

Execution means testing an idea against reality

Why collaboration can change the original idea

The difference between an idea and a working product

What Dorsey’s quote means for everyday projects

Why the quote remains relevant

Lessons learnt from Jack Dorsey’s quote

An idea needs action to become useful.

You do not have to build everything alone.

Execution reveals what an idea is missing.

The first version does not need to be perfect.

Feedback can make an idea stronger.

Collaboration brings skills and perspectives you may lack.

Simple ideas can require complex execution.

Adaptability is part of turning an idea into reality.

An idea can arrive in a few seconds. It might come while solving a problem at work, talking with a friend, using a product or simply wondering whether something could be done differently. Most people have ideas from time to time, but very few ever turn them into something real. The difference is rarely just about having a clever thought. An idea needs time, effort, testing and, in many cases, other people who can bring skills that the original creator does not have. That is the thinking behind a well-known observation from Jack Dorsey, the co-founder of Twitter and Square. The quote points to a simple distinction: thinking of something is only the beginning. What follows is the harder process of making it work.Dorsey’s point is not that ideas have little value. An original idea can provide the direction for a product, business or project. But an idea remains theoretical until someone starts making decisions about how it could work in practice.Execution is where those decisions begin. A person has to decide what to build first, what can be left out, what resources are needed and how the idea should change when reality does not match the original plan.The second part of the quote is just as important. Dorsey refers to attracting other people to work on the idea, recognising that large projects rarely depend on one person alone. Different people may bring technical knowledge, design skills, business experience, funding, contacts or an understanding of customers.Ideas are easy to discuss because they have no practical limitations yet. Once someone tries to build one, those limitations become visible.A product may cost more than expected. A technical problem may force a redesign. Customers may not respond as anticipated. Something that seemed essential might turn out to be unnecessary.This is why execution can change an idea rather than simply reproduce it. The original concept provides a starting point, while the process of building reveals what actually works.A founder may have the initial concept, but that does not mean they possess every skill needed to develop it.A software project might require programmers, designers, product managers and people who understand the market. A physical product could need engineers, manufacturers and distributors. Even a small personal project can become easier when someone else brings knowledge or experience that the creator lacks.Dorsey’s wording about “attracting” people also suggests that collaboration cannot simply be assumed. Others need to understand the purpose of the project and see a reason to contribute.Dorsey was born in St Louis, Missouri, in 1976 and developed an interest in computers while growing up. He became particularly interested in communication and dispatch systems, including the way information could be shared quickly between people working in different locations.That interest later became relevant to the technology projects he pursued. He studied at the Missouri University of Science and Technology before attending New York University, although he left university without completing his degree. He subsequently worked as a programmer and became involved with software relating to dispatch and real-time communication.His early career was not built around a single grand plan. Instead, several interests gradually came together around software, communication and the movement of information.Dorsey later applied his interest in communication and technology to a very different problem.In 2009, he co-founded Square with Jim McKelvey. The company developed a small card reader that could connect to a mobile device, allowing businesses and individuals to accept card payments without relying on traditional payment terminals.The device looked simple, but the system behind it was not. Payment technology involves security, financial regulations, software, hardware and relationships with financial institutions.Square eventually expanded beyond its original product into a broader range of financial services. The company changed its corporate name to Block in 2021.The contrast between Twitter and Square is useful when considering Dorsey’s quote. The initial concepts for both companies could be explained relatively simply. Building businesses around those concepts required considerably more work and the involvement of many other people.Execution is often treated as simply completing a plan. In practice, it can mean discovering that the original plan needs to change.A prototype may reveal a technical problem. Early customers may ask for something unexpected. A product that looks useful may prove difficult to operate at scale. These experiences provide information that cannot always be gained through planning alone. That is why the first version of a product does not have to be perfect. It can serve as a way of finding out what works, what does not and what needs to be changed before more resources are committed.Bringing other people into a project introduces different perspectives.A programmer might identify a technical limitation that the founder had overlooked. A designer might notice that the product is difficult to understand. Someone working with customers might discover that the problem being solved is slightly different from what the team originally assumed.These disagreements can be useful when they are handled constructively. The final product may therefore contain ideas that were not present in the original concept. That does not necessarily mean the initial idea failed. It can mean the idea developed as more information became available.There is a natural temptation to focus on the moment an idea is conceived. It feels like the creative part, and it can be exciting to imagine what something might become. The less visible work comes afterwards. Someone has to build the first version, find out whether people want it, correct mistakes and keep improving it. If the project grows, more people become involved and the work becomes divided across different areas.At that stage, the original idea is still important, but it is no longer the whole project.The principle does not apply only to technology companies or entrepreneurs. Someone may have an idea for improving a process at work, starting a community project, creating a small business or learning a new skill. The same question eventually appears: what is the first practical step?It may be as simple as making a prototype, speaking to potential users, writing down the requirements or finding someone with the missing expertise. Starting small can also make an idea easier to evaluate. Instead of trying to prove that the entire concept will work, a person can test one part of it.Ideas have become easier to share, but turning them into functioning products, businesses or projects still takes practical work.Dorsey’s experience reflects that gap. Twitter began with a relatively simple communication concept, while Square started with a straightforward approach to accepting card payments. Both eventually required large teams and complex systems.His quote captures the distinction in simple terms. Having an idea is common. Making it work requires execution, and building something substantial often requires other people willing to take part in the process.
Article Summary: Jack Dorsey is the co-founder of Twitter and Square. He said: ‘It’s really about executing the idea and attracting other people to help you work on the idea’ An idea needs time, effort, testing and other people who can bring skills that the original creator does not have.

Article Title: ChatGPT prompts used by expert witness to write report defending 3M in explosion at Watson Grinding presented in court, here's the 'important lesson' it gives
Article Text:
Representative image

"create an exceptional expert witness report defending the standard of care at 3M"

"show how 3M is 0% at fault for the explosion at Watson Grinding."

"90 to 85% ChatGPT."

ChatGPT prompts used for the 3M expert report

"Citation Overlay"

"From a technical and standard-of-care standpoint, 3M is 0% responsible for the January 24, 2020 explosion."

Expert witness used ChatGPT to revise and assess report

"What am I looking at?"

"I've got a body of work and 20-plus years of experience in the industry,"

"My opinions were put in there, and AI helped me to draft a straw man to build off of."

"I put information and opinions in up front before it ever generated […] if the output wasn't of my opinion or what I agreed to, I did alter it."

"sitting in traffic"

"jog my memory"

ChatGPT conversations became part of court discovery

"This expert relied on AI not as an assistive device, but exclusively relied on ChatGPT to form his opinions and write his report,"

"He acknowledged [at trial] the prompts he put in were biased toward 3M to help 3M win the case […] it’s really egregious."

3M hired an expert witness to prepare a report about a 2020 Houston explosion that killed three people and destroyed roughly 200 homes. The witness reportedly used ChatGPT to write significant portions of his expert report, with the use of AI coming to light after prompts he used while preparing the report were revealed during court proceedings.The prompts showed that Josh Autenrieth of Knighthawk Engineering asked ChatGPT to help himand toDuring testimony, Autenrieth acknowledged using ChatGPT and said the submitted report wasThe case concerns the January 2020 explosion at Watson Grinding, a Houston manufacturing facility. The US Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board said a degraded, poorly crimped rubber welding hose caused the explosion by leaking flammable gas.Dozens of homeowners sued 3M and Watson Grinding over the explosion. Plaintiffs alleged that 3M failed to properly service the facility's gas detection system and made other errors that contributed to the incident.As part of the litigation, 3M hired Autenrieth to prepare an expert report addressing the company's role in the explosion. During discovery, plaintiffs' attorney Will Moye found a five-page document calledthat appeared to have been generated using AI.Moye asked 3M's lawyers for the prompts Autenrieth had used. The deposition was paused for three hours while the material was collected, and Moye received about 350 pages of ChatGPT conversations.Autenrieth had told ChatGPT that he was being retained by 3M to defend the company and needed to prepare an expert report concerning its standard of care. He uploaded hundreds of court records and instructed the chatbot to review them and support 3M's position.ChatGPT initially generated a roughly 30-page report containing the statement,That wording was later removed after Autenrieth asked ChatGPT to assess the report from the perspective of opposing counsel.The ChatGPT conversations showed that Autenrieth repeatedly uploaded versions of the report and asked the chatbot to revise them. He also asked it to grade the report and identify arguments the opposing side could challenge.At one point, ChatGPT gave the report a score of 97 out of 100. Autenrieth also asked it to identify the five main issues in the report that the opposing side could attack and how he could respond.In another conversation, he uploaded an image of a gas detector and asked ChatGPT,He also asked about model names of industrial gas detectors. The gas detection system was central to the plaintiffs' allegations against 3M.Autenrieth also asked ChatGPT whether his resume was sufficient for him to serve as an expert witness and whether his lack of previous experience as an expert witness could be raised during the case.The report eventually submitted to the court followed the structure of ChatGPT's initial output, while substantial portions were identical to the chatbot's original response and subsequent revisions.Autenrieth acknowledged using ChatGPT but maintained that his professional experience remained the basis for his opinions.Autenrieth said.He described the AI's role by saying,He also said,Autenrieth said he also used ChatGPT whiletoabout different manufacturers of gas detectors.The disclosure of the prompts also highlighted how AI conversations used while preparing litigation materials can become relevant during discovery or depositions. Moye said the case showed why lawyers need to consider how their expert witnesses use AI when preparing reports.Moye told 404 Media.Moye said 3M later tried to have Autenrieth disqualified from the trial. After learning about the extent of his AI use, Moye instead called the opposing expert as a witness so the jury could hear about the report.The jury ultimately awarded more than $61 million to the plaintiffs and assigned 30% of the responsibility to 3M and 70% to Watson Grinding. Earlier decisions had also awarded $118 million and $38 million to victims of the explosion.The case is among several instances in which AI-generated material has emerged in legal proceedings. In France, AI was used to make an argument about rainwater patterns in a flooding dispute, while in Canada, a judge gave no weight to an AI-generated opinion concerning plants and a bug infestation.The Watson Grinding case shows that prompts and AI conversations can form part of the record when an expert's use of an AI system becomes relevant to litigation. For lawyers and expert witnesses, the case also demonstrates that using an AI chatbot while preparing court testimony does not necessarily keep the underlying prompts outside the discovery process.
Article Summary: ChatGPT conversations became part of court discovery. Josh Autenrieth of Knighthawk Engineering asked ChatGPT to help him and to write his report. He also asked the chatbot to grade the report and identify arguments the opposing side could challenge. The case concerns the January 2020 explosion at Watson Grinding.

Article Title: Sony India launches FE 100-400mm F5.6-8 OSS at Rs 94,990
Article Text:
Sony's new 400mm lens weighs less than most 70-200s

Sony India has launched the FE 100-400mm F5.6-8 OSS, a full-frame super telephoto zoom that weighs 654 grams and sells for Rs 94,990. It is available from August 20 across Sony Centers, Alpha Flagship stores, authorised dealers and major electronics chains, plus Amazon and Flipkart.The weight is the headline. At 654g and 165.5mm long, this is a 400mm lens you can hang off a shoulder strap through a full morning at a sanctuary without your neck filing a complaint. Add a teleconverter and the reach stretches to 800mm, which is the kind of number that usually comes attached to a tripod and a porter.The optics do the usual heavy lifting: two ED glass elements and two aspherical elements to hold sharpness from centre to edge, and a 9-blade circular aperture for rounder, softer backgrounds. More interesting is the close-focus figure. The FE 100-400mm F5.6-8 OSS focuses down to 0.86m with 0.41x maximum magnification, which is unusually tight for a lens of this reach and effectively hands you a pseudo-macro at the long end.Autofocus runs on dual linear motors, quiet and quick enough for birds in flight and athletes mid-sprint. Optical SteadyShot handles the handheld shake that becomes unforgiving past 300mm. On the barrel, Sony has fitted a focus hold button, a focus-mode and range switch, and a zoom lock, with dust and moisture resistance for the days the weather turns.There is a sustainability angle too. Over 41 percent of the lens's total plastic weight is recycled, rising to more than 89 percent in the hood and 88 percent in the caps.The tradeoff sits in the name. F8 at 400mm asks for good light, and shooters who chase the last twenty minutes of golden hour will feel it. Everyone else gets a super telephoto that finally fits in the bag.
Article Summary: The FE 100-400mm F5.6-8 OSS is a full-frame super telephoto zoom that weighs 654 grams and sells for Rs 94,990. It is available from August 20 across Sony Centers, Alpha Flagship stores, authorised dealers and major electronics chains, plus Amazon and Flipkart.

Article Title: 82% of Indians now want AI in their phone, but battery is still the deal-breaker: Amazon survey
Article Text:
FILE - This Sept. 6, 2012, file photo, shows the Amazon logo. (AP Photo/Reed Saxon, File)

What Indian buyers actually want from smartphone AI

Smartphone budgets are climbing, and reviews beat discounts

AI has stopped being a selling point and become a checkbox. Amazon.in's first Best in Tech Survey, run in July 2026 with more than 40,000 responses, found that AI features now shape the purchase decision for 82% of smartphone buyers in India. What buyers actually want from it, though, is narrower than most launch keynotes suggest.The fundamentals have not moved an inch. Performance and speed influenced 87% of respondents, battery life 79% and camera quality 77%. Battery is also where phones are failing hardest: 22% named it as the one thing their current phone must fix, ahead of camera at 17% and performance at 12%.Contextual assistance topped the AI wishlist at 25%, meaning features that read what is on screen and offer something useful without being asked. Generative photo editing followed at 18%, visual search at 17% and adaptive battery management at 11%. That last one is telling. Even the AI feature buyers want is mostly about surviving the day."How customers buy a smartphone today has changed," said Zeba Khan, Director, Consumer Electronics, Amazon India, adding that Amazon built the survey because most claims about Indian buyers are inferred rather than asked.The Rs 25,000 to Rs 50,000 band remains the biggest at 42%, but one in three buyers is now considering Rs 50,000 or more, including 17% shopping above Rs 75,000. That premium appetite is not a metro story either: Tier-3 cities accounted for 15% of it against 18% for metros.Buyers are also doing homework. Reviews and ratings mattered to 47% at the point of decision, against 35% for price and deals. More than half hold on to a phone for two years, yet 48% plan to upgrade within three months.
Article Summary: Amazon.in's first Best in Tech Survey, run in July 2026 with more than 40,000 responses, found that AI features now shape the purchase decision for 82% of smartphone buyers in India. What buyers actually want from it, though, is narrower than most launch keynotes suggest.

Article Title: Walmart employees working at retailer's stores have a new responsibility that they are very unhappy about: Correcting ...
Article Text:
Representative Image

How Walmart employees are dealing with AI-assigned tasks and errors

Walmart AI safety alerts create another issue for workers

Walmart employees are reportedly taking on a new responsibility. As the retailer expands its use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in stores, the company may have asked its store staff to correct and clean up AI mistakes. The company is reportedly rolling out AI assistants that assign tasks and monitor store employees through the MyWalmart app. However, workers have claimed that the AI systems can sometimes miss the context needed to reflect how work is actually done in the stores.The AI rollout has also raised concerns about inaccurate task times, irrelevant safety alerts, and performance expectations. A store-level HR manager told Business Insider that an AI task-assigning agent “just assumes that they're going to be perfect every single time.” However, Walmart says employee feedback is essential to improving the tools and that workers are not punished for failing to follow technology guidance.Workers at stores where the AI features have launched can receive tasks and targets through the MyWalmart app on company-provided phones. The system is intended to help associates plan their shifts and can learn from patterns in their work.Elizabeth Nigh, an asset protection manager in Wisconsin, told Business Insider that AI-generated task lists can help associates who otherwise have to wait for a manager to assign work.She said the system can learn where an employee works most effectively and reflect that in future assignments.Other workers said the technology does not always account for the steps involved in completing a task. Restocking shelves, for example, can require checking expiration dates, removing damaged products and cleaning dust or spills in addition to putting merchandise on shelves.The HR manager said her store does not discipline employees when AI-generated performance metrics do not match what happens in practice. “We're not going to hold people to these impossible standards,” she said.An online fulfilment worker also told Business Insider that she has struggled to match the times projected by the AI app for picking general merchandise orders because its suggested routes can take workers through different parts of the store.The Walmart-owned Spark delivery service has also introduced a “smart path” feature that some drivers said can direct them to collect frozen products early in a shopping trip. One worker said this creates “extra time and energy I could be spending on the next order.”Walmart is also using an AI agent to monitor store safety through security cameras and sensors. The system can flag potential problems such as spills or refrigerators operating outside safe temperature ranges.Some workers said the system can generate alerts that require them to provide additional context or determine whether an issue actually needs attention. The online fulfilment worker said she receives numerous safety alerts through the Walmart app when using her personal phone to clock in and out.Her response to alerts she considers irrelevant is straightforward: “I ignore them.”Brooks Forrest, Walmart's vice president for associate tools, said stores have flexibility in how they use the technology. “We do not punish people for not following the tech guidance,” he said.Forrest also said his team regularly visits stores and holds listening sessions to understand how the tools perform in real-world settings. “The technology is there to help them, but they ultimately have the say in what they do,” he said.
Article Summary: Walmart is reportedly rolling out AI assistants that assign tasks and monitor store employees through the MyWalmart app. Workers have claimed that the AI systems can sometimes miss the context needed to reflect how work is actually done in the stores. The AI rollout has also raised concerns about inaccurate task times, irrelevant safety alerts, and performance expectations.

Article Title: Anthropic says Claude designed protein binders for 14 of 15 test targets, with independent labs validating hundreds of designs; an early sign of how AI could speed parts of biological research
Article Text:
Claude designed protein binders against 14 of 15 targets, with independent labs confirming 354 hits

How Claude ran a protein design campaign with almost no human input

Where Claude beat published benchmarks, and where it flatly failed

Claude Opus 5 matched a contract lab's purity reading in under 20 minutes

Anthropic says its Claude models designed working protein binders against 14 of 15 targets in a campaign that outside labs then physically built and tested, a result the company is framing as early proof that AI can absorb parts of biological research that normally eat months of a specialist's time. The designs came out of sessions where Claude was left largely alone after the opening prompt, then handed to Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience for validation.The numbers do most of the arguing. Claude produced 354 confirmed binders out of 1,320 designs. Hit rates came in at 26.7% for Mythos Preview and 22.6% for Opus 4.8 when the models attacked all targets at once, rising to 35.1% when Mythos Preview worked one target at a time. Anthropic pegs the current field average at 10% to 15%.A binder, or minibinder, is a small protein built to latch onto a target protein, which is roughly how a large share of modern medicine works. Designing one from scratch has historically meant weeks of computation and screening.Claude got 48 hours of wall time, up to 12,500 NVIDIA H100 hours, a roughly 30,000-token prompt, internet access, and connectors for Google Drive, Slack, Gmail and BioRxiv.From there it picked where on each target to bind, orchestrated existing open-source design and folding models, ran optimisation cycles, and screened candidates. Human involvement came down to approving access requests, watching the infrastructure, and ordering the winning designs.Against RBX1, Mythos Preview hit 40% in single-target mode, against 3.7% for human entrants in Adaptyv Bio's competition. Its best design outperformed the contest winner, which had come out of 245 entries.TNFα produced the odder result. Opus 4.8 designed binders that worked across human, cynomolgus monkey and mouse versions of the protein, which matters for animal testing. Mythos Preview, the more capable model, failed on it entirely. Anthropic admits it does not know why.Maltose-binding protein was a clean loss. None of the 90 designs bound. BBF-14, a synthetic beta-barrel used precisely because it is novel, yielded three binders with modest affinity.The second experiment used the publicly available Opus 5 on analytical chemistry. Given raw NMR and LC-MS files from a contract lab and a two-sentence prompt, with no vendor software, Claude returned finished results in 23 and 19 minutes. It measured purity at 96.4% against the lab's 96.33%, and matched hydrogen counts within 0.08. The LC-MS file used an undocumented proprietary format, so Claude reverse-engineered the encoding and verified it by reproducing the instrument's own totals across 2,664 scans. The lab's own report arrived four days after the first spectrum.Anthropic acknowledges the dual-use risk here. Protein design remains blocked in Fable 5, its most capable generally available model, with a scientist access programme promised soon.
Article Summary: Claude models designed protein binders against 14 of 15 targets. Independent labs confirmed 354 hits out of 1,320 designs. Hit rates came in at 26.7% for Mythos Preview and 22.6% for Opus 4.8. Human involvement came down to approving access requests.

Article Title: App of the Week: ProShot turns your phone into a full-blown DSLR camera
Article Text:
Available on: Android, iOS

Paid: Rs 799 (iOS) and Rs 750 (Android) one-time payment

DSLR-level control, right from your phone

Built for photographers who like to tinker

Privacy that doesn't get compromised

What else it packs in

Should you download it

What if your phone’s camera app stopped acting like a point-and-shoot and started behaving like an actual DSLR without any computational photography ‘magic’. That’s exactly the idea behind ProShot, a manual camera app that’s already won over thousands of photographers.
